title: Songbook and Letters
premise: Quentin Montrose, a lighthouse keeper's granddaughter who writes romance novels under a man's name, has spent ten years training her heart into obedience after a betrayal at the orchard she inherited. When a legal quirk places her estranged first love, Elias Wren, as co-owner on the same stubborn deed, the two are forced to settle the property — and their history — before the harvest festival. As Quentin drafts and burns letter after letter she cannot send, she discovers the 'betrayal' was a sacrifice Elias made to save her family's land. At the festival's closing night, Quentin finally speaks the rehearsed sentence aloud, choosing love over the duty of guardedness, and they sign the deed together as partners in every sense.
about_author: U. M. Iversen is the pen name of a former maritime archivist who spent years cataloguing lighthouse logs and unsent letters along the northern coast. They write romances about people who mistake discipline for peace.

chapters.title: The Deed That Would Not Die
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV. A county clerk's error surfaces: the orchard deed lists both Quentin and Elias Wren, the man who vanished from her life a decade ago. She storms to the records office, armed with legal arguments and rehearsed indifference, but the clerk notes the deed is valid until jointly settled. Emotional beat: controlled fury cracking into dread as she realizes she must face him.

chapters.title: What the Tide Returned
chapters.summary: Alternating POV begins with Elias arriving at the orchard, carrying a weathered satchel of letters he never sent. Their first meeting is all clipped civility over fence lines and falling fruit, but a storm forces them to shelter in the orchard house together. Emotional beat: old tenderness flickering under mutual armor; Quentin notices he still knows how she takes her tea.

chapters.title: Letters in the Wall
chapters.summary: Elias's POV. Repairing the orchard house wall, they uncover letters Quentin's grandmother hid — revealing that Elias left because he quietly paid off the Montrose debts, trading his inheritance for hers. Quentin confronts him; he refuses apology, insisting duty required it. Emotional beat: betrayal inverted into devotion, and Quentin's trained heart failing its training.

chapters.title: The Sentence at Festival's End
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV. On the festival's final night, with lanterns over the orchard and the deed unsigned on the table between them, Quentin abandons her rehearsed speech and says the sentence she has practiced for ten years: that she never stopped loving him. They sign as partners. Emotional beat: release — memory transformed from wound to foundation.
